title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination, Part 1: Stepping Forward Quietly
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
series: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true spiritual growth and stability come from embracing a simple yet profound practice of trusting in the present moment, rather than trying to control or achieve something specific. By letting go of reactivity and embracing silence, participants can develop greater trust and inner peace, even in the face of difficult emotions or memories. This approach encourages individuals to cultivate a sense of grounding and awareness that can be applied to everyday life, leading to greater stability and freedom.

sentences.text: Yesterday I was thinking about what to say, and it had a sort of frantic quality, you're trying to think of something to say.

So to give you a little more of a flavor of where this is coming from, this expression, great faith, great doubt, great determination, I thought I would share a little bit of an essay, or it's probably a transcribed talk, by one of the mid-20th-century Rinzai masters who were instrumental in bringing practice to America.
This is Koun Yamada Roshi.
He said or wrote:
*First, great faith, second, great doubt, third, great determination.
These are like the three legs of a tripod.
It is uncertain whether we can accomplish the Dharma if one of these three legs is missing.
If all three are present, however, we will be more likely to miss the ground with a hammer than we would be to miss enlightenment.*
You're not too likely to miss the ground if you just hit it with a hammer.
See, you need these three to accomplish the Dharma.
He goes on.
*The first condition, great faith, means believing without any doubt that you are intrinsically awake, that all beings are intrinsically awake.
You also believe that seeing into your own nature means discovering something that you have already been using from morning to night without even realizing it.
Because seeing into your own nature is you discovering yourself.
You cannot fail to experience it.

Great faith also means believing that every person is in the process of eventually achieving supreme enlightenment, and trusting that if we ask for help from the three treasures, Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, we will definitely get it.
Lastly, great faith means that we believe in the teachings of our Zen teacher.*
We're pretty good in alignment so far with Yamada Roshi: really having deep faith in our intrinsic awakening.
He goes on.
*This great root of faith is not a tepid faith.
There's a thoroughgoing belief that we will settle for nothing less than complete awakening, and it is rooted firmly in the ground like a huge tree, immovable in the face of even the strongest gale.
When this root of faith is present, there's nowhere for demons to get a foothold.*
We're getting a little more intense.

There are some interesting differences.

*Now what is great doubt?
The type of doubt being referred to here is not an intellectual doubt such as we have when asking the meaning of a koan.

When practicing with mu, for example, as long as we think there is something called ourselves that is practicing, we have not quite achieved great doubt.
When we are truly meditatively absorbed in mu and mu itself is practicing mu, but we are still aware of this, we're still self-conscious in our practice, it is still not fully great doubt.
Harada Roshi used to say mu, mu's, mu.*
